Hello and thanks for your contribution!

I'm not sure this is the right approach conceptually. Currently, export annotations in GDScript are exclusive, meaning one export annotation cannot be used in conjunction with another. However, you add the `PROPERTY_USAGE_REQUIRED` flag, which can be used in conjunction with other export hints and usage flags (for example, if you want to use `@export_range` and `@export_required` simultaneously on the same property). Export annotations in GDScript mostly correspond to core export hints, not usage flags. The only exception is `@export_storage`, for which it doesn't make sense to change the export hint since the property is hidden in the Inspector.

A similar issue arose when we tried to implement editor-only property export; see the `@no_storage` PR #101117. Modifier annotations that don't export a property themselves, but are used in conjunction with other export annotations, are a completely new concept. We're still unsure of their necessity, as well as their nomenclature and naming. Currently, you can also use `@export_custom` to specify custom export hints and usage flags. While this is more cumbersome, this annotation is specifically intended for advanced use cases and can be used when a corresponding annotation doesn't exist in GDScript.

Regarding the core feature, the `PROPERTY_USAGE_REQUIRED` usage flag, I'm not entirely sure that's conceptually correct either. I understand that you want to create a short syntax that doesn't require `@tool`, but this essentially duplicates the functionality of `_get_configuration_warnings()`. We can't require properties at the language level, and it would be overly strict if the editor refused to save (or `PackedScene` refused to instantiate) a scene with unfilled required properties. This is purely a warning system.

You can also use editor plugins to validate scenes without having to use `@tool`. See the https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/3004 in which the last participant mentions a plugin they created.

Finally, I'd like to point out that the number of possible usage flags is quite limited: 64, or perhaps even only 32. We currently use 29 usage flags. We should be careful when allocating usage flags.

Hey, 

Thanks for replying.

I completely agree with your concerns for the enum values being limited. I hope more people weigh in on this.

As for the behaviour for export annotations that you mentioned, I understand what you mean although I don't completely agree. `@export_required` has the exact same functionality as `@export`, and the only addition is that it automatically includes the `PROPERTY_USAGE_REQUIRED` flag into the usages when the annotations are being parsed.

I will be looking into the editor tools method that you mentioned and possibly looking into if we can extend the parser (easily and safely without breaking anything) to include this functionality in a different way.

I hope more people weigh in on this, but if this PR is rejected I'm fine with it. It was just fine to try and implement this :D

Thank for you clarifying.
The reason I chose Usage over Hint is because I saw that the Hint is exclusive and I didn't think the "required" validation was something that, in the long run, should be an exclusive annotation. But your concerns of introducing a new Usage enum value when we have limited spots, as well as whether the annotation should be an "addition"/"modifier" are valid.

In the short term, I originally thought that adding `@export_required` as its own exclusive annotation would be fine, but I am now going to consider better ways to include this functionality. 

I will also consider the `@required` annotation that can be tacked on, like the `@no_storage` annotation. Although I don't love that syntax. Would hate to see `@export @required @no_storage ... var thing: type` down the line.

I was curious, so I double-checked how the enum backing type is resolved.
> 1) Declares an unscoped enumeration type whose underlying type is not fixed (in this case, the underlying type is an implementation-defined integral type that can represent all enumerator values; this type is not larger than int unless the value of an enumerator cannot fit in an int or unsigned int. If the enumerator-list is empty, the underlying type is as if the enumeration had a single enumerator with value ​0​. If no integral type can represent all the enumerator values, the enumeration is ill-formed).

From [cppreference enum](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/enum.html).

I suppose this means that for most platforms the enum is probably a 32 or 64 bit integer right now, and as soon as we pass that many flags, it will switch to a 64 bit underlying type (probably a long or long long), since c++ doesn't make guarantees about default integer sizes in bits, only the smallest width in bits.

Not sure what ramifications this has on adding more flags to the enum.

I have nothing to add to what I said above. I mentioned `@required` as a possible alternative to the proposed `@no_storage`, but I'm not sure about that either (my approval of that PR only concerns the implementation; the concept of modifier annotations still requires discussion by the GDScript team).

Regarding your PR, its scope is somewhat broader, as it affects not only GDScript but also Core+Editor. In my opinion, there are two issues to discuss:

* (Core) Is `PROPERTY_USAGE_REQUIRED` necessary as a shorthand in addition to `_get_configuration_warnings()`, or is it redundant? Maybe there are some alternative ideas?
* (GDScript) Discussion of the concept of annotations that modify export info in conjunction with other export annotations, rather than being used on their own. Naming of such modifier annotations.

So, for now, I'll hold off on reviewing the actual implementation of your PR until the above-listed conceptual issues are clarified and consensus is reached. Let's wait for more people to express their opinions on this matter. If you'd like, you can ask other contributors for their opinions in the [Contributors Chat](https://chat.godotengine.org).

I feel like a better approach to this would be to make nullable @export fields _always_ required by default (as that is the safest and most likely scenario) and then have an @optional annotation instead. I would be putting @required on all my @exported vars as a best practice and this would end up being boilerplate.

Additionally, I feel like it would be a lot easier to miss a var you want to be required by accident than miss a var you want to be optional. The first time you run your game, you'll know if you accidentally left off @optional where you want it. It's catching a bug at compile time rather than runtime, and I feel like compile time errors should always be preferred.

Please surround GDScript annotations in backticks, \`like this\`, to avoid mentioning users due to GitHub's special syntax. These users have been fortunately inactive, but that may not be the case next time.
